meta.title: Who really said "They're Cheering Us Both, You Because Nobody Understands You, and Me Because Everybody Understands Me"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Chaplin’s own 1933 account credits the observation to one of Einstein’s sons, in different words. The famous wording first appears in a 1947 memoir by a man who was not there.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'They're Cheering Us Both, You Because Nobody Understands You, and Me Because Everybody Understands Me'?
meta.ogDescription: Not the exchange as told. Chaplin’s first-hand 1933 article credits Einstein’s son; the familiar wording comes from a second-hand 1947 memoir.

answer.label: Not Chaplin’s line as quoted — Chaplin credited Einstein’s son
answer.authorDates: Albert Einstein’s sons · Chaplin did not record which one spoke
answer.sourceLine: The only first-hand account is Chaplin’s own. Writing in Woman’s Home Companion in October 1933, he describes an evening at Einstein’s flat and attributes the observation about their two kinds of fame not to himself but to Einstein’s son: “You are popular because you are understood by the masses. On the other hand, the professor’s popularity with the masses is because he is not understood.” Einstein had two sons, Hans Albert and Eduard, and Chaplin does not say which one he meant. The polished version everyone quotes — Chaplin delivering the line in a car amid a cheering crowd — first appears in 1947, in the memoir of Einstein’s physician János Plesch, who was not present when the words were spoken. Quote Investigator ↗ judges the Plesch telling probably inaccurate.

source.excerpt: We sat down to delicious home-baked tarts made by Mrs. Einstein. During the course of conversation, his son remarked on the psychology of the popularity of Einstein and myself. “You are popular,” he said, “because you are understood by the masses. On the other hand, the professor’s popularity with the masses is because he is not understood.”
trail: The earliest evidence is Chaplin’s own travel series. In Woman’s Home Companion for October 1933 he describes visiting Einstein’s “modest flat”, and gives the remark about their two kinds of popularity to Einstein’s son — not to himself the citation ↗.

The wording everyone repeats enters print fourteen years later, in János: The Story of a Doctor (1947) by Einstein’s physician János Plesch, translated by Edward Fitzgerald: Chaplin drives Einstein through Hollywood, the crowd cheers, and Chaplin says “They’re cheering us both … you because nobody understands you, and me because everybody understands me”. Plesch was not there the 1947 text ↗.

The later biographies descend from Plesch rather than from Chaplin. Carl Seelig’s Albert Einstein: A Documentary Biography (1956) cites Plesch by name; Denis Brian’s Einstein: A Life (1996) traces back to Seelig; and Walter Isaacson’s Einstein: His Life and Universe (2007) footnotes Seelig and Brian the chain of borrowing ↗.
Theodore Huff’s 1951 biography Charlie Chaplin is the exception that proves the point: its version matches the 1933 magazine article, quoting Einstein’s son rather than Chaplin the 1951 citation ↗.
source.cutTag: Charlie Chaplin, Woman’s Home Companion, October 1933
source.excerptNote: The earliest known account, written by the one participant who published a first-hand version. The setting is Einstein’s flat, not a car; the speaker is Einstein’s son, not Chaplin; and the wording is not the one in circulation.
source.rightsNote: Quote sparingly and attribute. The passage reproduced above is Charlie Chaplin’s own prose, first published in Woman’s Home Companion in October 1933 — after the 1930 cut-off for the United States public domain — so it remains in copyright, as do the 1947 Plesch memoir, its 1947 English translation by Edward Fitzgerald, and the later biographies quoted here. We have not been able to establish which party holds those rights today and so do not name one. This is not legal advice.

author.name: Charlie Chaplin
author.heading: Why it gets pinned on Chaplin
author.metaLine: 1889–1977 · English comic actor, filmmaker and composer
author.bio: Sir Charles Spencer Chaplin is the obvious candidate for the line, and that is exactly the problem: it is far too good a Chaplin joke not to be given to Chaplin. The irony is that he is also the only participant who left a first-hand account — and in it he hands the observation to somebody else. A better-worded second-hand version has been out-competing his own testimony ever since.

copyAttribution: Not the exchange as usually told. In Chaplin’s own first-hand account (Woman’s Home Companion, October 1933) the observation is made by one of Einstein’s sons, at Einstein’s flat: "You are popular because you are understood by the masses. On the other hand, the professor’s popularity with the masses is because he is not understood." The familiar Chaplin wording first appears in János Plesch’s 1947 memoir; Plesch was not present.

misattribution.heading: The attribution problem
misattribution.intro: Two people were in the room and neither of them is the one usually quoted. The story is not fabricated — Chaplin and Einstein really did meet, and really were cheered together — but the line has migrated to the wrong mouth and been improved on the way.

items.why: Chaplin published his own account of the evening in October 1933 and gave the remark to Einstein’s son. The version that puts it in Chaplin’s mouth reaches print in 1947, from someone who was not present both accounts ↗.

items.scope: The other half of the dialogue
items.why: A widely circulated two-part version has Einstein speaking first — “What I most admire about your art is your universality … you don’t say a word, yet the world understands you!” No source of any kind supports that half; Quote Investigator calls the dialogue probably inaccurate the assessment ↗.

Chaplin’s first-hand account puts the conversation at Einstein’s flat, over home-baked tarts, after a dance performance. The cheering-crowd staging comes from the 1947 memoir and from Seelig’s 1956 retelling of it the two settings ↗.
Chaplin names no son, and Einstein had two — Hans Albert and Eduard — so even the correct attribution stops one step short of a name QI on the ambiguity ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: Chaplin’s own 1933 article credits one of Einstein’s sons; the famous wording is a second-hand 1947 improvement the evidence ↗.

context.heading: Why the wrong version won
lead: The Plesch version is simply the better anecdote. It has a crowd, a car, two of the most recognisable men alive, and a punchline delivered by the funnier of them. Chaplin’s own telling has tarts, a flat, and an unnamed young man making a shrewd remark. Only one of those survives retelling.

It is also a clean example of how citation chains launder a claim. Seelig cites Plesch, Brian follows Seelig, Isaacson footnotes both, and a Princeton University Press reference work points at a fourth biography — four respectable sources, one unverified origin, and the first-hand account sitting unread the whole time.
detailsBody: October 1933: Chaplin’s own article in Woman’s Home Companion. The remark belongs to Einstein’s son. This is the earliest evidence.
1947: János Plesch, Einstein’s physician, publishes the cheering-crowd version with Chaplin as speaker. Plesch was not there.
1951: Theodore Huff’s Charlie Chaplin follows the 1933 magazine account — the son, not Chaplin.
1956: Carl Seelig’s documentary biography retells Plesch by name, and places the scene at the City Lights premiere.
1996 and 2007: Denis Brian and Walter Isaacson each carry the line forward, footnoting Seelig and Brian rather than Chaplin.
2010: The Ultimate Quotable Einstein prints it and points to a 1997 biography for support.
context.pull: Chaplin wrote down what happened. The better story beat him to it anyway.

schema.verdictNote: Popularly credited to Charlie Chaplin. Chaplin’s own first-hand account (Woman’s Home Companion, October 1933) instead credits the observation to one of Albert Einstein’s sons, in different words; the familiar Chaplin wording first appears in János Plesch’s 1947 memoir, and Plesch was not present. Quote Investigator judges the Plesch telling probably inaccurate rather than disproven. A widely circulated two-part version also puts an unsourced line in Einstein’s mouth.

sourcesVerified.claim: QI: earliest evidence is Chaplin’s October 1933 Woman’s Home Companion article, which credits the fame observation to Einstein’s son; the familiar Chaplin wording first appears in Plesch’s 1947 memoir, page 211; Plesch was not present; QI believes the Plesch anecdote probably inaccurate; Huff 1951 matches the 1933 account; Seelig 1956, Brian 1996 and Isaacson 2007 descend from Plesch.
Charlie Chaplin (Sir Charles Spencer Chaplin Jr.) lived 16 April 1889 to 25 December 1977 and was an English comic actor, filmmaker and composer.
Albert Einstein lived 1879 to 1955; he is the other participant in the anecdote.
